rows: Hepatitis A cases require public-health assessment to reduce secondary infections.
Management should consider the infectious period and likely transmission setting.
Close contacts may need post-exposure prophylaxis according to current guidance.
Hepatitis A vaccine can be used for prevention and outbreak control.
Human normal immunoglobulin may be considered for eligible contacts under current guidance.
Food-handling, childcare and other higher-consequence settings require careful assessment.
Hygiene and sanitation measures help reduce faecal-oral transmission.
Clusters and outbreaks require coordinated case finding, communication and control.
A positive report or shared setting does not establish who transmitted hepatitis A.
Case and contact decisions require symptoms, laboratory, timing, vaccination, setting and public-health evidence.
Healthcare-worker bloodborne-virus management should protect patients while supporting affected workers.
Health clearance requirements depend on the role and exposure-prone procedures.
Hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV require pathogen-specific assessment.
Confidential testing and occupational-health pathways support safe management.
Restrictions or monitoring should be proportionate to viral and work-related risk.
Treatment response can affect whether exposure-prone procedures are permitted.
Sharps and exposure incidents require prompt reporting and clinical assessment.
Records and review should follow current national guidance.
A diagnosis or job title alone does not determine whether a healthcare worker can perform a procedure.
Decisions require role, procedure, pathogen, viral markers, treatment, monitoring and expert occupational-health evidence.
Potential rabies exposures require prompt risk assessment.
Assessment considers the animal, country, exposure category and person's prior immunisation.
Wounds should be cleaned promptly after a bite or scratch.
Rabies vaccine can prevent disease when given correctly after exposure.
Human rabies immunoglobulin may be indicated for specified high-risk exposures.
Post-exposure treatment should begin promptly and should not wait for symptoms.
Treatment schedules differ for fully immunised, non-immunised and immunosuppressed people.
Current UKHSA country-risk and immunoglobulin guidance should be used.
An animal bite or travel history does not automatically establish rabies exposure.
Treatment decisions require animal, location, wound, timing, immunisation, immune status and current UKHSA assessment.
Norovirus is highly infectious and commonly causes vomiting and diarrhoea.
Outbreaks are common in semi-enclosed settings.
Rapid recognition and reporting can support outbreak control.
People with symptoms should follow setting-specific exclusion and isolation advice.
Hand hygiene and environmental cleaning are important control measures.
Contaminated areas and equipment require suitable disinfection procedures.
Movement, admission or group-activity controls may be needed during outbreaks.
Outbreak closure should use current symptoms, timing and public-health criteria.
Vomiting or diarrhoea in a shared setting does not prove norovirus.
Outbreak conclusions require case definition, onset pattern, setting, laboratory, cleaning and public-health evidence.
